title: "Quarterback Play: Progressions, the Pocket, and Off-Script Football"
subtitle: "What the quarterback does in the three seconds after the snap, what he does when the three seconds run out, and how to measure the difference between quarterbacks"
description: "The quarterback's job after the snap, step by step: the protection check, the progression run on the clock of his feet, the anticipation throw, climbing, sliding and escaping the pocket, the scramble drill and off-script football, the throwaway and why it must not be intentional grounding, the checkdown as risk management, and the numbers that profile a passer (time to throw, aDOT, CPOE, EPA per dropback), ending with why the quarterback dominates a team's value."
glossary:
  "Climbing the pocket": "The quarterback stepping forward into the pocket, between his interior linemen, as the edge rushers are pushed past him, so that he can keep reading and throw from a clean spot instead of drifting back into the rush."
  Throwaway: "A pass the quarterback deliberately throws where nobody can catch it (out of bounds, or over a covered receiver's head) to avoid a sack or an interception: he gives up the down but keeps the yardage. It must be thrown so that it is not intentional grounding."
  "Scramble drill": "The offense's practiced rules for what receivers do when the quarterback leaves the pocket and is still looking to throw: short routes go deep, deep routes come back toward him, receivers work toward the side he runs to, spread out at different depths, and get into his line of sight."
  "Off-script play": {def: "A play that leaves its design: the quarterback escapes the pocket or holds the ball past the play's timing, and the result depends on improvisation (his and the receivers' scramble drill) rather than on the called routes.", aliases: ["Off-schedule play"]}
  "Anticipation throw": "A pass released before the receiver is open, usually before he makes his break, aimed at the spot where the window between defenders will be when the ball arrives."
  Checkdown: "The short, safe throw at the end of a progression, usually to a running back or tight end underneath the coverage, taken when the deeper reads are covered. It trades a chance at a big gain for a near-certain small one."
  CPOE: {def: "Completion percentage over expected: a passer's completion rate minus the rate a model expects from how difficult his throws were (depth, location, down and distance, and in some models how open the receiver was). Positive means he completed more passes than throws like his usually produce.", aliases: ["Completion percentage over expected"]}

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import os
import logging
import textwrap

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import animation
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, RegularPolygon, Rectangle
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

import gridiron.play as gplay
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, style

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
# gridiron's default ball speed (18 yd/s) averages a whole flight; the firm 20-25 yard throws in this
# chapter travel a little faster, so the simulated plays use 20.
gplay.BALL_SPEED = 20.0

GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight: reads, the quarterback's moves
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]   # a ring for the defender who decides the read
RED = style.SERIES[7]      # danger: a rush that got home, an illegal throw
SPLIT = 1.6                # center-to-guard and guard-to-tackle spacing, as in the rest of the book
OL_KEYS = ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"]
NONROUTE = {"LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "DE", "DT", "NT"}


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line():
    """The five offensive linemen (only the center is lettered, to keep the box readable)."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, (i - 2) * SPLIT, "C" if k == "C" else "") for i, k in enumerate(OL_KEYS)]


def four_rush():
    """A generic four-man rush: two ends outside the tackles, two tackles inside."""
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")]


def timed(p, key, way, kind="path"):
    """Script a player exactly: `way` = [(t, d, w), ...] absolute spots reached at t seconds after the
    snap. Repeating a spot means 'stand there until t'. (gridiron's route helpers run at a fixed speed;
    the quarterback's clock is the subject of this chapter, so here every move is timed by hand.)"""
    cur = np.array(p._cur(key), dtype=float)
    tc, wait = 0.0, 0.0
    if any(a.key == key for a in p.actions):          # continue from where his earlier moves end
        tc = max(0.0, float(p._compile()[0][key][-1, 0]))
    for t, d, w in way:
        nxt = np.array([d, w], dtype=float)
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(nxt - cur)))
        if dist < 1e-3:
            wait += t - tc
        else:
            p._add(kind, key, [tuple(cur), tuple(nxt)], speed=dist / (t - tc), delay=wait)
            wait = 0.0
            cur = nxt
        tc = t
    return p


def frame_field(ax, p, lateral, window):
    ylo, yhi = sorted((p.ball_y - lateral[0], p.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    return Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=p.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                 lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=p.to_go)


def XY(fld, p, d, w):
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def dot(ax, x, y, side, label, ppy, r=0.9, ring=None, alpha=1.0, z=8):
    """One player: offense a filled blue circle, defense an outlined orange square."""
    if side == "off":
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=z, alpha=alpha))
        tc = "white"
    else:
        ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=r * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=z, alpha=alpha))
        tc = style.INK
    if ring:
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r * 1.65, fc="none", ec=ring, lw=1.7, zorder=z - 0.5))
    if label:
        fs = max(4.6, min(8.5, ppy * (1.15 if len(label) <= 1 else 0.85)))
        ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=z + 2)


def place_labels(ax, xs, ys, labels, fs=6.8, offs=None):
    """Greedy label placement for scatter charts: try offsets around each point until the label hits no
    point, no earlier label and stays inside the axes."""
    fig = ax.figure
    fig.canvas.draw()
    ren = fig.canvas.get_renderer()
    pts = ax.transData.transform(np.column_stack([xs, ys]))
    box = ax.get_window_extent(ren)
    offs = offs or [(5, 3), (5, -9), (-5, 3), (-5, -9), (6, -3), (-6, -3), (0, 6), (0, -12), (9, 8), (-9, 8),
                    (9, -13), (-9, -13), (12, 0), (-12, 0)]
    placed = [t.get_window_extent(ren) for t in ax.texts]          # never cover text already on the chart
    if ax.get_legend() is not None:
        placed.append(ax.get_legend().get_window_extent(ren))
    for x, y, lab in zip(xs, ys, labels):
        for dx, dy in offs:
            t = ax.annotate(lab, (x, y), xytext=(dx, dy), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=fs, color=style.INK,
                            ha="left" if dx > 0 else ("right" if dx < 0 else "center"), zorder=4)
            bb = t.get_window_extent(ren).expanded(1.04, 1.1)
            ok = (not any(bb.contains(px, py) for px, py in pts) and not any(bb.overlaps(o) for o in placed)
                  and box.contains(bb.x0, bb.y0) and box.contains(bb.x1, bb.y1))
            if ok:
                placed.append(bb)
                break
            t.remove()
    return placed


def football(ax, x, y):
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), 1.0, 0.62, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=11))


def arrow(fld, p, pts, color=GREEN, lw=1.8, ls="-", head=10, z=9, alpha=1.0):
    """A path through (d, w) points with an arrowhead at the end."""
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1] + (xs[-1],), ys[:-1] + (ys[-1],), color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z,
                solid_capstyle="round", alpha=alpha)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color, lw=0,
                                     shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, zorder=z, alpha=alpha))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK, fs=7.0, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True):
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92) if box else None)


def badge(ax, x, y, n, state, fs=8.0):
    """A numbered read. wait: not looked at yet; now: his eyes are here; done: looked at and passed over."""
    fc, ec, tc = {"wait": (style.SURFACE, style.MUTED, style.INK_2), "now": (GREEN, GREEN, "white"),
                  "done": (style.GRID, style.BASELINE, style.MUTED)}[state]
    ax.text(x, y, str(n), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, fontweight="bold", color=tc, zorder=13,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.22", fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.1))


def clean(ax):
    """Static diagrams drawn with Play.draw: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def moment(ax, p, t, lateral, window, rings=None, plan=None, ghosts=(), trail_keys=None, r=0.9):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, faint trails of where he has been, the ball, and (optionally)
    the called routes as faint grey dashes, so a single panel shows both the plan and the present."""
    fld = frame_field(ax, p, lateral, window)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    lo, hi = sorted(lateral)
    inside = lambda d, w: window[0] + 0.6 <= d <= window[1] - 0.6 and lo + 0.6 <= w <= hi - 0.6  # noqa: E731
    for pts in (plan or {}).values():
        xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
        xs, ys = zip(*xy)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 2)), alpha=0.75, zorder=2)
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=6, color=style.MUTED, lw=0,
                                     alpha=0.75, zorder=2))
    if t > 0:
        ts = np.linspace(0, t, 32)
        for k, pl in p.players.items():
            if (pl.pos in NONROUTE) if trail_keys is None else (k not in trail_keys):
                continue
            pts = np.array([p.position(k, tt) for tt in ts])
            if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
                continue
            xs, ys = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]))
            if pl.side == "off":
                ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.1, alpha=0.5, zorder=3)
            else:
                ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), alpha=0.8, zorder=3)
    for d, w, text in ghosts:
        x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
        ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.72, fc="none", ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=6))
        if text:
            ax.text(x, y - 1.45, text, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=max(5.0, ppy * 0.7), color=style.INK_2,
                    zorder=6)
    for k, pl in p.players.items():
        d, w = p.position(k, t)
        if inside(d, w):
            dot(ax, *XY(fld, p, d, w), pl.side, pl.label, ppy, r=r, ring=(rings or {}).get(k))
    thrown = [(to, te) for kind, to, te in p.ball_events if kind == "pass" and t > te]
    if thrown:
        bd, bw = p.ball_position(t)
        sd, sw = p.ball_position(thrown[0][1])
        rd, rw = p.position(thrown[0][0], t)
        caught = np.hypot(bd - rd, bw - rw) < 0.4
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(XY(fld, p, sd, sw), XY(fld, p, bd, bw), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=8,
                                     color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9, shrinkA=0,
                                     shrinkB=9 if caught else 2))
        football(ax, *XY(fld, p, bd + (0.3 if caught else 0.0), bw - (1.25 if caught else 0.0)))
    elif t > 0.15 and "QB" in p.players:
        qd, qw = p.position("QB", t)
        football(ax, *XY(fld, p, qd + 0.3, qw - 1.2))
    return fld


def eyes(fld, p, t, target, color=GREEN):
    """The quarterback's eyes: a dashed line from him to the player he is reading."""
    (qd, qw), (rd, rw) = p.position("QB", t), p.position(target, t)
    x0, y0 = XY(fld, p, qd, qw)
    x1, y1 = XY(fld, p, rd, rw)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (4, 2)),
                                     shrinkA=7, shrinkB=9, zorder=7))


def strip(draw, times, notes, ncols=2, width_in=6.5, aspect=1.0, note_lines=2):
    """Print stand-in for an animation: numbered panels with a caption under each."""
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * aspect + 0.2 + 0.16 * note_lines)),
                             squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        draw(ax, t)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"), fontsize=8.2,
                     color=style.INK_2, loc="left", pad=3)
        ax.text(0.5, -0.01, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.1,
                color=style.INK, linespacing=1.2)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2, w_pad=0.8)
    return fig


def video(draw, times, notes, t_end, width_in=5.6, aspect=1.0):
    """Web version of the strip: every tenth of a second, with the strip's captions as running titles."""
    import shutil
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * aspect + 0.6))

    def update(t):
        ax.clear()
        draw(ax, t)
        cur = [n.replace("\n", " ") for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        head = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(textwrap.fill(head + ("   " + cur[-1] if cur else ""), 92), fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK,
                     loc="left")
        return []

    frames = list(np.round(np.arange(0.0, t_end + 0.05, 0.1), 2))
    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def play_out(draw, times, notes, t_end, ncols=2, aspect=1.0, note_lines=2, width_in=6.5):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if PDF:
        strip(draw, times, notes, ncols=ncols, aspect=aspect, note_lines=note_lines, width_in=width_in)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(draw, times, notes, t_end, aspect=aspect)


BOX_W = 3.9   # the tackle box: Rule 3-25 puts its edges at the OUTSIDE shoulders of the tackles, not their centers


def tackle_box(ax, fld, p, back):
    """The shaded tackle box (pocket area), from the line back to depth `back`."""
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in [(-0.7, -BOX_W), (-0.7, BOX_W), (back, BOX_W), (back, -BOX_W)]]
    ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.09, ec=PURPLE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.4))


def pass_set(p, depths=(-2.6, -1.7, -1.4, -1.7, -2.6), t=0.8):
    """The five linemen set (tackles deeper and wider than the interior) and hold."""
    for k, dd in zip(OL_KEYS, depths):
        w0 = p.players[k].w
        timed(p, k, [(t, dd, w0 * 1.15)], "block")
    return p
```

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (load the quarterback data used in this chapter)"}
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]          # the FTN charting era, all completed seasons
PC = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "play_type", "qb_dropback", "qb_scramble", "sack",
      "pass_attempt", "passer", "passer_id", "posteam", "epa", "qb_epa", "success", "cpoe", "cp", "air_yards",
      "yards_after_catch", "receiving_yards", "complete_pass", "interception", "down", "ydstogo", "qb_spike",
      "rusher", "passing_yards", "pass_touchdown"]
raw = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PC)
raw = raw[raw.season_type == "REG"]
# every dropback: pass attempts, sacks and scrambles (spikes removed)
db = raw[(raw.qb_dropback == 1) & (raw.qb_spike != 1)].copy()

# FTN charting: which read the ball went to, out of the pocket or not, throwaways
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(SEASONS).to_pandas()
ftn = ftn.rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})[
    ["game_id", "play_id", "read_thrown", "is_qb_out_of_pocket", "is_throw_away", "is_interception_worthy",
     "is_qb_fault_sack"]]
ftn["read_thrown"] = ftn.read_thrown.astype(str).str.strip()
part = nfl().load_participation(SEASONS).to_pandas().rename(columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id"})[
    ["game_id", "play_id", "time_to_throw", "was_pressure"]]
db = db.merge(ftn, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left").merge(part, on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="left")
db["oop"] = db.is_qb_out_of_pocket.fillna(False).astype(bool)
db["throwaway"] = db.is_throw_away.fillna(False).astype(bool)

# How every dropback ended, in mutually exclusive groups (order matters)
END_NAMES = ["Throw to the first read", "Throw to a later read", "Checkdown", "Designed throw (mostly screens)",
             "Scramble-drill throw", "QB scramble (he runs)", "Throwaway", "Sack", "Interception"]
conds = [db.sack == 1, db.qb_scramble == 1, db.interception == 1, db.throwaway,
         db.read_thrown == "1", db.read_thrown == "2", db.read_thrown == "CHK", db.read_thrown == "SD",
         db.read_thrown == "DES"]
names = ["Sack", "QB scramble (he runs)", "Interception", "Throwaway", "Throw to the first read",
         "Throw to a later read", "Checkdown", "Scramble-drill throw", "Designed throw (mostly screens)"]
db["ending"] = np.select(conds, names, default="Other")
END = db.groupby("ending").agg(n=("qb_epa", "size"), epa=("qb_epa", "mean"), succ=("success", "mean"))
END["share"] = END.n / len(db)
END = END.loc[END_NAMES]

# Checkdowns: what they gain, and what they do on third down
CHK = db[db.ending == "Checkdown"]
CHK_COMP, CHK_AY, CHK_YAC = CHK.complete_pass.mean(), CHK.air_yards.mean(), CHK.yards_after_catch.mean()
t3 = db[db.down == 3]
long3, short3 = t3[t3.ydstogo >= 7], t3[t3.ydstogo <= 3]
CHK3_LONG = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Checkdown", "success"].mean()
R1_3_LONG = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Throw to the first read", "success"].mean()
CHK3_SHORT = short3.loc[short3.ending == "Checkdown", "success"].mean()
CHK3_LONG_EPA = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Checkdown", "qb_epa"].mean()
SACK3_LONG_EPA = long3.loc[long3.ending == "Sack", "qb_epa"].mean()

# Out of the pocket
OOP_SHARE = db.oop.mean()
EPA_IN, EPA_OUT = db.loc[~db.oop, "qb_epa"].mean(), db.loc[db.oop, "qb_epa"].mean()
SACK_IN, SACK_OUT = db.loc[~db.oop, "sack"].mean(), db.loc[db.oop, "sack"].mean()
# ...and the confound: quarterbacks mostly leave BECAUSE the pressure has arrived. Compare like with like on
# pressured dropbacks (FTN's pressure flag, 2023-2025; the 2022 flag comes from a different source)
pz = db[db.season >= 2023]
PRESS_IN, PRESS_OUT = pz.loc[~pz.oop, "was_pressure"].eq(True).mean(), pz.loc[pz.oop, "was_pressure"].eq(True).mean()
pzp = pz[pz.was_pressure.eq(True)]
PSACK_IN, PSACK_OUT = pzp.loc[~pzp.oop, "sack"].mean(), pzp.loc[pzp.oop, "sack"].mean()
OOP_MIX = db[db.oop].ending.value_counts(normalize=True)
OOP_BAD = OOP_MIX.reindex(["Throwaway", "Sack", "Interception"]).sum()
OOP_RUN, OOP_SD = OOP_MIX["QB scramble (he runs)"], OOP_MIX["Scramble-drill throw"]
# whose sack? FTN marks the sacks its charters blame on the quarterback; pressure-to-sack rate by passer
QB_FAULT = db.loc[db.sack == 1, "is_qb_fault_sack"].eq(True).mean()
P2S = pzp.groupby("passer_id").agg(name=("passer", "first"), press=("sack", "size"), p2s=("sack", "mean"))
P2S = P2S[P2S.press >= 200].sort_values("p2s")
P2S_ALL = pzp.sack.mean()
# throwaways and the CPOE model: most have no completion probability, so they are left out of nflverse CPOE
TA_CP_SHARE = db.loc[db.throwaway & (db.pass_attempt == 1), "cp"].notna().mean()

oq = db.groupby("passer_id").agg(name=("passer", "first"), n=("qb_epa", "size"), oop=("oop", "mean"))
oq = oq.join(db[db.oop].groupby("passer_id").agg(n_out=("qb_epa", "size"), epa_out=("qb_epa", "mean")))
oq = oq.join(db[~db.oop].groupby("passer_id").agg(epa_in=("qb_epa", "mean")))
OQ = oq[(oq.n >= 800) & (oq.n_out >= 150)].copy()
OQ["gain"] = OQ.epa_out - OQ.epa_in
N_BETTER_OUT = int((OQ.gain > 0).sum())
```

Third-and-8, fourth quarter. The quarterback takes the snap in the shotgun, drops, and looks hard to his
left. Then his head snaps to the middle of the field. He bounces once on his back foot, then again. The two
defensive ends have run around his tackles and are closing from behind him, so he takes two quick steps
*forward*, into the space they left. Now a defensive tackle shoves a guard backward into his face, and the
quarterback spins out to his right and runs toward the sideline. His receivers, who had been running set
routes, suddenly do something else: the one who was deep turns and runs back toward him, the one who was
short takes off deep, and a receiver from the far side of the field races across. Four and a half seconds
after the snap, the ball floats over a cornerback who is still turning around, and the receiver catches it
alone near the sideline. The analyst says, "That's what the great ones do." What, exactly, did he do? Why did he step
*up* and not back? How did the receivers know where to go? And when none of it works, why is throwing the
ball into the seats sometimes the best play he can make? This chapter is about the quarterback's three to
four seconds: what he is doing with his eyes, his feet and his judgment, on schedule and off it.

**You'll be able to…**

- Narrate a quarterback's dropback from the snap to the throw: the protection check, the progression on the
  clock of his feet, and the moment he decides to leave the pocket.
- Count, on a replay, how many reads a quarterback went through before he threw, by following his eyes and
  his hitch steps.
- Tell climbing, sliding and escaping the pocket apart, and say why stepping *up* usually beats drifting back.
- Predict where receivers will go when the quarterback scrambles, using the scramble-drill rules.
- Say when a throwaway or a checkdown is the right decision, and why a throwaway must avoid intentional
  grounding.
- Profile a quarterback from four numbers (time to throw, aDOT, CPOE and EPA per dropback), and explain why
  the position dominates a team's value.

**How to read the diagrams.** The conventions of the rest of Part 4, plus a few for this chapter:

- **Players.** Offense blue circles, defense orange squares; *left* and *right* are always the offense's. Q is the
  quarterback, R the running back, X and Z the outside receivers, H the slot receiver and Y the tight end; the
  five linemen are the blue circles at the line, with only the center lettered. On defense E is an end, T a
  tackle, M and W the Mike and Will linebackers, \$ the slot (nickel) cornerback, C a cornerback, FS and SS the
  safeties.
- **Lines on the field.** The dark blue line across the field is the line of scrimmage; the thick yellow-orange one
  is the line to gain (the first-down line), drawn whenever the down and distance matter to the decision.
- **Green belongs to the quarterback:** his eyes (a dashed green line to the man he is reading), his moves in the
  pocket, and his **numbered reads**, which ride beside the receiver they belong to. A white number is a read he
  hasn't reached, a green one is where his eyes are now, a grey one a read he looked at and passed over.
- **Rings.** A purple ring marks the defender who answers the read (or, in @fig-anticipation, the defender
  nearest the catch); a green ring the player to watch (the quarterback in the drills, the receiver who gets
  the ball); a red ring the rusher who got home.

The moving pictures add three more: faint lines are where a player has been (solid blue for offense, dashed
orange for defense), grey dashes are the routes as they were *called*, and a dashed brown arrow is the ball in
flight.

## The quarterback's clock

Every dropback is a race against a clock the defense controls, and the quarterback runs a fixed sequence of
jobs against it. Coaches teach the sequence by tying each job to a moment in the drop, so that the quarterback's
feet tell him what his eyes should be doing.

Much of the work is done before the clock starts. Before the snap he has identified the Mike and set the
protection ([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)), read the defense's alignment for which half of the
field he expects to work ([The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)), and checked
whether the look calls for a change of play or a shot down the field (a subject of
[Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)). After the snap, here is
the order, for an ordinary dropback pass from the shotgun.

1. **At the snap: the protection check.** Before he looks at a single receiver, the quarterback answers one
   question: did more rushers come than the protection can block? If yes, the ball goes *now* to the
   [hot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) receiver or a receiver who
   [sight-adjusted](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sight-adjust) his route, before any progression starts. The
   protection call has already told him which rusher is his: the one the line leaves unblocked by design if he
   comes, whom the quarterback must beat with a quick throw. So this check takes a glance, not a study.
2. **The drop: read 1.** If the rush is covered, his eyes go to the first read as his feet go back, and the
   decision comes as the last step of the drop lands: open, and the ball comes out as his back foot plants;
   covered, and he moves on.
3. **Each hitch step: the next read.** If read 1 is covered, he takes a short step forward, the *hitch step* of
   [Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) (a step, not to be confused with the hitch route),
   which resets his feet so he can throw again, and his eyes move to read 2. Another hitch step, read 3. Each
   hitch step takes about half a second.
4. **The last read: the checkdown.** The final look is to a back or tight end a few yards past the line, the safe
   throw that keeps the play from becoming a loss.
5. **After that: off schedule.** If the ball still isn't out, the play has left its design. The quarterback now
   has to manage the pocket (step up, slide, or escape), and decide among a scramble, an improvised throw, a
   throwaway, or taking the sack.

The bottom half of @fig-qb-clock is the part to remember. The first-read throw leaves the quarterback's hand at
a median of 2\.3 seconds; a throw to a later read, about
0\.6 seconds after that; and the throwaways and
scramble-drill throws at the far right of the chart, after three seconds, when the rush has usually arrived. The
checkdown is the odd one: it is the *last* look on paper, yet its median is no later than a second read's. Two
things pull it early. On many quick and half-field plays the back is read 2 or 3, not the last of four or
five, so his turn comes fast; and some checkdowns are thrown before the deeper reads had a chance, the "bad checkdown" the
[checkdown section](#checkdown) warns about. About 27% of checkdowns left the
quarterback's hand inside two and a half seconds. Every step down the list costs time, and, as you'll see, value.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Tying the eyes to the feet** solves a problem that sounds trivial and isn't: in the chaos of a rush, how does a
quarterback know when to give up on a receiver? Counting seconds doesn't work with three hundred pounds of
defensive tackle in his face. Feet do. "Last step, read one; hitch step, read two; hitch step, checkdown" turns a judgment
into a rhythm he can practice ten thousand times, and it keeps him on the same clock as his receivers, whose
routes are timed to the same drop ([Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)).

**What it gives up:** freedom. A quarterback who throws on rhythm throws to where the play says, not to where a
receiver happens to be open. When the defense takes away the design, a rhythm passer can be stuck; that is
where the second half of this chapter, the off-script game, comes in.
:::

## The progression, live

[Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) drew a progression as numbers on a play diagram.
Watched in real time it looks different: the numbers light up one at a time, on the beat of the quarterback's
feet, and at each one he is asking a yes-or-no question that one defender answers. The play is
[dagger](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dagger), drawn as [Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) drew
it, against the [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) coverage it was built to beat.

::: {#cell-fig-progression .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
LOS, TOGO = 40, 10


def upto(p, key, way, t_stop, kind="drop"):
    """Script a defender along `way` [(t, d, w), ...] but only until t_stop, the moment he reacts to the ball."""
    cut, prev = [], (0.0, *p._cur(key))
    for t, dd, ww in way:
        if t <= t_stop:
            cut.append((t, dd, ww))
            prev = (t, dd, ww)
        else:
            f = (t_stop - prev[0]) / (t - prev[0])
            cut.append((t_stop, prev[1] + f * (dd - prev[1]), prev[2] + f * (ww - prev[2])))
            break
    timed(p, key, cut, kind)


def dagger(throw_t=2.4, react=0.5):
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]
    # Quarters from a nickel: two safeties at 12 over the slots, corners off, three underneath plus the nickel
    dfn = four_rush() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -5.0, "W"),
                         D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 7.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 9.0, "SS"),
                         D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "C"),
                         D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=TOGO)
    pass_set(p)
    for k, (d, w) in {"LE": (-1.7, -4.6), "NT": (-0.6, -0.9), "DT": (-0.7, 2.0), "RE": (-1.7, 4.6)}.items():
        timed(p, k, [(0.8, d, w)], "rush")
    # quarterback: five-step drop from the gun to 9 yards, then a hitch step every half second
    timed(p, "QB", [(1.95, -9.0, 0.0), (2.4, -8.4, 0.0), (2.9, -8.0, 0.0)])
    # back: checks for a blitzer, then releases to sit underneath as the checkdown
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.5, -5.2, 2.4), (1.4, -5.2, 2.4), (2.4, 2.5, 3.2), (2.9, 3.2, 2.4)], "route")
    timed(p, "Y", [(3.3, 23.5, 8.2)], "route")                                          # seam
    timed(p, "Z", [(2.35, 15.6, 15.0), (2.55, 16.0, 13.6), (3.7, 16.0, 4.0), (4.4, 16.0, -1.5)], "route")  # dig
    timed(p, "X", [(2.8, 20.0, -15.0)], "route")                                        # go
    timed(p, "H", [(1.6, 10.5, -8.5), (1.9, 9.5, -9.3)], "route")                       # curl
    p.pass_to("Z", t=throw_t)
    _, catch = p.pass_target_spot()
    tr = throw_t + react
    # Quarters: the strong safety reads Y and carries the seam; the nickel sinks under it; the Mike sits at ten
    # yards with his eyes on the quarterback and only later walls off the crosser; the corner stays over Z
    upto(p, "SS", [(0.9, 12.8, 8.9), (1.9, 15.6, 8.6), (2.8, 20.5, 8.4), (3.6, 23.5, 8.3)], tr)
    upto(p, "NB", [(1.2, 8.5, 8.2), (2.2, 11.0, 8.4), (3.0, 12.5, 8.4)], tr)
    upto(p, "MIKE", [(1.3, 8.0, 2.4), (2.3, 9.6, 3.0), (2.8, 10.0, 3.0), (3.4, 12.5, 1.8)], tr)
    upto(p, "RCB", [(1.0, 8.5, 15.2), (2.3, 15.2, 15.4), (2.8, 17.6, 13.8), (3.6, 18.2, 8.5)], tr)
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.3, 8.0, -5.0), (2.3, 9.0, -4.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.0, 12.0, -9.0), (2.2, 12.5, -8.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(2.8, 18.0, -15.5)], "drop")
    # once the ball is in the air, they break on it (after a reaction time) and stop a step short
    for k, spd in (("MIKE", 4.5), ("SS", 4.0), ("NB", 4.0), ("RCB", 4.5)):
        start = np.array(p.position(k, tr))
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(np.array(catch) - start)))
        stop = start + (np.array(catch) - start) * max(0.0, (dist - 0.9) / dist)
        timed(p, k, [(tr + max(0.05, (dist - 0.9) / spd), *stop)], "drop")
    return p, catch


def catch_time(p, key="Z"):
    for kind, to, te in p.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass":
            start = np.array(p.ball_position(te))
            ta = te + 0.5
            for _ in range(4):
                ta = te + float(np.hypot(*(np.array(p.position(to, ta)) - start))) / gplay.BALL_SPEED
            return ta


PLAN = {"Y": [(-1.5, 8.5), (23.5, 8.2)], "Z": [(-0.7, 15.0), (15.6, 15.0), (16.0, 13.6), (16.0, 3.0)],
        "RB": [(-5.0, 1.6), (-5.2, 2.4), (2.5, 3.2), (3.2, 2.4)], "X": [(-0.7, -15.0), (20.0, -15.0)],
        "H": [(-1.5, -8.5), (10.5, -8.5), (9.5, -9.3)]}
prog, _ = dagger()
T_CATCH = catch_time(prog)
LAT, WIN = (-18.0, 18.0), (-11.5, 26.0)
# each numbered read rides beside its receiver: (receiver, offset in d, offset in w)
BADGES = {1: ("Y", 0.2, -2.4), 2: ("Z", 0.3, -2.4), 3: ("RB", -2.0, 1.6)}
T_SET, T_HITCH = 1.95, 2.4


def draw_prog(ax, t):
    s1 = "wait" if t < 1.0 else ("now" if t < T_SET + 0.2 else "done")
    s2 = "wait" if t < T_SET + 0.2 else "now"
    ring = ({"SS": PURPLE} if 1.0 <= t < T_SET + 0.2 else
            ({"MIKE": PURPLE} if T_SET + 0.2 <= t < T_HITCH + 0.4 else {}))
    fld = moment(ax, prog, t, LAT, WIN, rings=ring, plan=PLAN)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for n, st in ((1, s1), (2, s2), (3, "wait")):
        key, dd, dw = BADGES[n]
        rd, rw = prog.position(key, t)
        badge(ax, *XY(fld, prog, rd + dd, rw + dw), n, st, fs=max(6.0, ppy * 1.0))
    if 1.0 <= t < T_SET + 0.2:
        eyes(fld, prog, t, "SS")
    elif T_SET + 0.2 <= t <= T_HITCH + 0.05:
        eyes(fld, prog, t, "MIKE")


TIMES = [0.0, T_SET, T_HITCH, round(T_CATCH, 1)]
NOTES = ["Snap: four rush, four blocked.\nNo hot throw; eyes go to read 1.",
         "Last step of the drop: read 1, the seam.\nThe safety carries Y deep. No.",
         "Hitch step: read 2. The Mike sits at ten\nyards: the window is open. Ball out.",
         "Caught in the window. Read 3,\nthe checkdown, was never needed."]
play_out(draw_prog, TIMES, NOTES, t_end=T_CATCH + 0.4, aspect=(WIN[1] - WIN[0]) / (LAT[1] - LAT[0]), width_in=6.1)
```

A progression in real time (simulated play), first-and-10 (the yellow-orange line is the line to gain). The call is dagger to the right, the two-high beater of Dropback Concepts: Y runs up the seam to pull the deep defenders, Z runs a deep dig (an in-breaking route at about 16 yards) behind him, and R is the checkdown. The defense plays Quarters, two safeties deep, and rushes four. The quarterback takes a five-step drop from the shotgun. Panel 1: at the snap he counts the rush (four, all blocked: no hot throw). Panel 2: on the last step of his drop his eyes are on read 1, the seam, and its key, the strong safety (ringed), who carries Y deep, as Quarters tells him to: no. Panel 3: on his hitch step he moves to read 2. Its key is the Mike (ringed), who has sat down at about ten yards with his eyes on the quarterback, so the window behind him will be open; the ball comes out as Z breaks. Panel 4: the ball arrives in that window, under the safety and over the linebackers. Read 3 was never needed. The numbered reads ride beside their receivers; X's go and H's curl on the left (grey dashes) are not part of this progression.
:::
:::


Three things are happening in @fig-progression that you can't see in a static play diagram.

**Every read has a key defender.** [Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) separated two kinds
of read: a *progression*, which looks at receivers one at a time, and a *defender read*, which watches one
defender. Dagger is a progression, but even on a progression each look is answered by one defender, and good
quarterbacks look at him. At read 1 the question is not really "is Y open?" but "what is the safety on Y's side
doing?" In Quarters that safety is taught to carry the inside receiver if he goes deep, so a seam route is open
only if he doesn't, and here he does. At read 2 the question is the Mike linebacker: has he dropped deep enough to
take away the dig, or is the window behind him open? Here he sits at ten yards with his eyes on the quarterback,
and the safety is gone with Y, so the space at sixteen yards between them is empty. Which defender is the key on
which play depends on the coverage, and that is a subject of its own:
[Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd) teaches it, once Part 6 has
taught the coverages themselves.

**The order is a ranking of risk and reward, and a timetable.** Read 1 is the biggest gain the play can produce (a
seam is a touchdown if the safety guesses wrong); read 2 a solid one; read 3 a small, safe one. A progression runs
from the most valuable throw the defense might allow to the least dangerous one, so that the quarterback takes the
big play when it is there and the safe one when nothing else is. It is also a schedule: each route is built to come
open just as his feet arrive at that read. Z's dig breaks at about 2.4 seconds because that is when the hitch step
lands. Many coaches sum it up as *deep to short*, but the timetable is the real rule, and on quick concepts the
order starts short: stick and slant-flat key one underneath defender and throw whichever of two short routes he
leaves ([The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd)).
Dagger is a full-field read in the language of [Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd); on a
half-field read the order is shorter, and what the quarterback saw before the snap can decide which half he
starts on.

**The ball comes out before the receiver is open.** In panel 3 the dig hasn't broken yet; Z is still running
straight up the field. The quarterback throws anyway, because he has seen what he needed: the Mike is in front
of the window, not in it, and the safety is committed to the seam. That kind of throw has a name.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden every receiver carries a button icon, the camera sits high behind the quarterback, and you can see the
whole field at once and press the button of whoever looks open. A real quarterback sees through a forest of
six-and-a-half-foot linemen with helmets bouncing in his face, from eye level, and can usefully look at one area
at a time. That is why a progression exists at all: he can't scan everything, so the play tells him what to look
at, in what order, and when to give up on each look. When an analyst says a quarterback "got through his
progression," he means the quarterback looked at the right things, in the right order, on time, which is much
harder than pressing the right button.
:::

### Anticipation: throwing to a window that isn't there yet

An [**anticipation throw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-anticipation-throw) is a pass released before
the receiver is open, usually before he makes his break, aimed at the spot where the window between defenders
will be when the ball gets there. It is the bigger, riskier cousin of the timing route of
[Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): a timing route is thrown to a fixed spot on a fixed
step, while an anticipation throw is a judgment, made on any route, about where defenders *will be* in a second.

Why throw to a receiver who isn't open? Because the ball takes time to get there. A firm 20-yard throw is in the
air for about a second, and in a second a linebacker can close five yards. A window that is open when the
quarterback *sees* it is often closed by the time the ball arrives. What makes it a judgment rather than a timing
route is what he reads in the half second before he lets go. On dagger the timing is in the play; the decision is
the Mike. If the Mike is sinking as Z stems upfield, eyes turned to the receivers, he is going to be standing in the
window, and the throw dies. If he sits with his eyes on the quarterback, he will be in front of it. The quarterback
has to make that call while Z is still running straight upfield.

::: {#cell-fig-anticipation .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def sep_at_catch(p):
    tc = catch_time(p)
    z = np.array(p.position("Z", tc))
    dd = {k: float(np.hypot(*(np.array(p.position(k, tc)) - z))) for k in ("MIKE", "SS", "NB", "WILL", "RCB")}
    k = min(dd, key=dd.get)
    return tc, k, dd[k]


early, _ = dagger(2.4)
late, _ = dagger(2.9)
SEP = {}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.4))
LAT2, WIN2 = (-7.5, 19.5), (-10.5, 24.0)
for ax, p, ttl, key, lab_off in ((axes[0], early, "Anticipation: out at 2.4 s, as he breaks", "early", (-1.9, 3.6)),
                                 (axes[1], late, "“See it, throw it”: out at 2.9 s", "late", (-0.4, -4.4))):
    tc, k, dist = sep_at_catch(p)
    SEP[key] = (tc, dist)
    fld = moment(ax, p, tc, LAT2, WIN2, rings={k: PURPLE}, plan={"Z": PLAN["Z"]})
    z, dfd = p.position("Z", tc), p.position(k, tc)
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, p, *z), XY(fld, p, *dfd)
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x0, y0), dist, fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.08, ec=PURPLE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=7))
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=PURPLE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (1, 1.2)), zorder=12)
    dot(ax, x0, y0, "off", "Z", fld.pts_per_yard(), r=0.9, z=13)      # the receiver on top of everyone
    name = {"MIKE": "the Mike", "NB": "the nickel", "SS": "the safety", "RCB": "the corner"}.get(k, k)
    say(fld, p, dfd[0] + lab_off[0], dfd[1] + lab_off[1], name, color=PURPLE, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
    say(fld, p, -7.0, 12.5, f"caught at {tc:.1f} s\nnearest defender {dist:.1f} yd", color=PURPLE, fs=7.2,
        weight="bold")
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.4, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
```

In the simulation the early throw is caught with the nearest defender
2\.4 yards away; the late one with a defender
0\.9 yards away, close enough to knock it down or catch it himself. The difference
is half a second, one hitch step.

A simulation only shows what it was told, and this one was told that defenders break on the ball when it is
thrown, not when they see the receiver break. So treat it as an illustration of the mechanism, not proof. The
proof that windows matter is in tracking data. Next Gen Stats measures, for every target, how far the receiver
was from the nearest defender when the ball arrived. Across 885 receiver-seasons with 50 or more
targets from 2018 to 2025, each extra yard of average separation went with about
3\.7 more percentage points of catch rate, at the same average depth of
target.[^ngs-sep] An anticipation throw is a way of buying that yard with the clock instead of the receiver's
speed.

The trade is just as plain. An anticipation throw is a bet on the future, made on information about the present:
the quarterback is predicting that the receiver will break where and when he is supposed to, and that the
defender he is reading will keep doing what he is doing. If the receiver slips, rounds his cut, or is held up,
the ball arrives at an empty spot, often into a defender's hands. And if the defender *was* disguising his
intentions, sitting shallow to bait the throw, the window was never going to open. Anticipation is therefore the
skill that most separates veteran quarterbacks from rookies: it takes years of reps with the same receivers to
know exactly where they'll be, and years of film to know what a linebacker's first two steps mean.

Coaches often say the young quarterback "needs to see it before he throws it." What they mean is that he is
throwing a beat late, waiting for the receiver to look open, which, as @fig-anticipation shows, is too late
against good defenses.

## The pocket: climb, slide, escape

The progression assumes a quarterback standing calmly at his launch point. He rarely is. A pocket is a moving
thing (the tackles giving ground, the interior bending), and the quarterback has to move inside it without
losing his eyes or his feet, so that he can still throw on time from wherever he ends up. Coaches name three moves.

::: {#cell-fig-pocket-moves .cell execution_count=6}

**Climb.** [**Climbing the pocket**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-climbing-the-pocket) means
stepping forward into the pocket, between the interior linemen, as the edge rushers are pushed past. It is the
single most important pocket skill, and it follows directly from the geometry of
[Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd): the tackles give ground on purpose and ride the ends on a wide arc
*behind* the launch point, while the guards and center hold firm in front. A quarterback who stays at his launch
point, or worse, drifts backward, walks into the spot where the ends' arcs finish. One who steps up two yards
lets the ends run past behind him, and throws from the cleanest spot on the field. Quarterback coaches drill the
idea endlessly: pressure from the outside is answered by moving *up*, not back.

**Slide.** When pressure comes from one side (an end who beat the tackle inside, a blitzer through a gap) and
the middle is still firm, the quarterback slides a yard or two the other way, keeping his shoulders square to the
line of scrimmage and his eyes downfield. A slide buys a half second without ending the play: he is still in the
pocket and can still throw to anyone in the progression.

**Escape.** When the pocket is gone, usually because the interior collapsed and the quarterback has nowhere to
step up into, he leaves. The usual escape lane is outside one of the tackles, on the side where an end rushed too
far upfield and was pushed past; it opens exactly because the tackle did his job. Escaping changes the play into
something else, which is the next section's subject.

All three moves are made with both hands on the ball. Quarterback coaches drill it as hard as the footwork:
a quarterback who carries the ball loose in one hand while he climbs or slides is the one who gets it knocked out
from behind by the end he never saw, the strip-sack.

The skill under all three is doing them *without looking at the rush*. A quarterback who drops his eyes to watch
the defensive end has stopped reading the coverage, and a quarterback who has stopped reading the coverage has
stopped running the play. Great pocket passers feel the rush (from the color at the edge of their vision, from
the sound, from the pressure on a lineman's back) and move their feet while their eyes stay downfield.
Coaches call this *pocket presence*, and it is one of the few things that clearly separates good quarterbacks from
bad ones, as @fig-climb shows in motion.

``` {.python .cell-code}
def climb_play():
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")], four_rush(), los=LOS, to_go=None)
    for k, way in {"LG": [(0.6, -1.8, -1.8), (2.6, -2.1, -1.8)], "C": [(0.6, -1.5, 0.0), (2.6, -1.8, 0.0)],
                   "RG": [(0.6, -1.8, 1.8), (2.6, -2.1, 1.8)]}.items():
        timed(p, k, way, "block")
    for sg, (lt, le) in ((-1, ("LT", "LE")), (1, ("RT", "RE"))):
        timed(p, lt, [(0.7, -2.6, 4.2 * sg), (1.3, -4.6, 5.0 * sg), (2.0, -7.2, 5.1 * sg), (2.6, -9.2, 4.4 * sg)],
              "block")
        timed(p, le, [(0.7, -1.4, 6.2 * sg), (1.3, -4.0, 6.5 * sg), (2.0, -7.2, 6.3 * sg), (2.6, -9.8, 5.3 * sg)],
              "rush")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.6, -0.5, -1.0), (2.6, -0.9, -1.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.6, -0.6, 2.0), (2.6, -1.0, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.95, -8.0, 0.0), (1.7, -8.0, 0.0), (2.25, -5.7, 0.2), (2.6, -5.6, 0.2)])
```

Climbing the pocket, in motion (simulated, the box only). Both ends rush wide around the tackles; the tackles kick back with them and push them deeper than the quarterback's launch point (the dashed circle), while the guards and center hold their ground against the two tackles. At about 1.8 seconds the ends are level with the quarterback: a drift backward would put him between them. He steps up into the cup instead and throws two yards further upfield, and the ends finish their arcs behind him.
:::
:::


::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A mobile quarterback should get out of the pocket whenever it gets crowded." Quarterback coaches teach the
opposite: don't leave a pocket that still works. Outside it he has fewer throws (he can see only half the field
and has to throw on the run), the rushers who were blocked are now chasing him unblocked, and the sideline is an
extra defender. The best scramblers in the league are good at *not* leaving until the pocket is gone. Then they are
devastating, as the next section shows.

Be careful with the obvious statistic here. In FTN's charting from 2022 to 2025, quarterbacks were sacked on
8\.3% of dropbacks once they were out of the pocket, against
6\.2% in it,[^ftn-oop] which looks like proof that leaving gets you sacked. It isn't,
because quarterbacks mostly leave *because* the pocket has already failed: from 2023 to 2025,
57% of out-of-pocket dropbacks were charted as pressured, against
24% of the rest. Compare like with like, pressured dropbacks only, and the ones
that got outside ended in a sack *less* often (15% against
26%). Once the pocket has collapsed, escaping is a rescue. What the charting can't
tell you is what leaving a pocket that was still good costs, because nobody charts whether it was still good. That
part of the rule rests on coaching judgment, not on this number.
:::

## Off-script football and the scramble drill

When the quarterback escapes the pocket, or holds the ball past the play's last read, the play has gone
**off script**. An [**off-script play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-script-play) (also called an
[**off-schedule play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-schedule-play)) is one that has left its design:
the called routes have run out, the protection has broken, and what happens next depends on improvisation.

Improvisation sounds like the opposite of coaching. It isn't. The quarterback improvises, but his receivers follow
rules, practiced every week, that tell them what to do when he starts running. Those rules are the
[**scramble drill**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scramble-drill). Every team has its own version and its
own vocabulary, but the core is nearly universal.[^scramble-rules]

Each rule has a reason.

- **Short goes deep, deep comes back.** Receivers spread out vertically so the quarterback has a choice of
  depths, and so that two receivers never end up in the same spot dragging their defenders with them. The deep
  receiver comes *back* because a quarterback throwing on the run cannot make a 40-yard throw accurately; the
  short receiver goes deep because the defenders near him have all turned to chase the quarterback, and the space
  behind them is empty. "Short" and "deep" are measured against the linebackers: in front of them is short, behind
  them is deep.
- **Go where he goes.** A quarterback running to his right can throw easily to his right and downfield, and only
  with difficulty back across his body to the left. (Throwing across your body on the run is one of the most
  dangerous throws in football, because the ball floats back toward the middle of the field where the defenders
  are.) So receivers work toward his side.
- **Backside receivers come across, deep.** A receiver on the far side can't stand still and wait; he runs back
  across the field behind the coverage, where defenders who have turned to chase the quarterback have left the
  deep middle.
- **The back leaks out; the linemen stay home.** A back who stayed in to block releases toward the scramble side,
  a yard or two past the line, as the last, safest throw. The linemen keep blocking whoever they have and do not
  drift downfield: if the quarterback then throws, a lineman more than a yard beyond the line is
  [ineligible downfield](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-ineligible-downfield), a foul that wipes out the
  completion ([RPOs](04-06-rpos.qmd)).[^ineligible]
- **Get into his line of sight and keep moving.** A receiver the quarterback can't see is not an option. Receivers
  find grass on a different level from their teammates and stay in his vision, and if he crosses the line of
  scrimmage to run, they stop running routes and start blocking. Nobody calls out "scramble": the cue is the clock.
  A receiver who reaches the end of his route without the ball turns to find the quarterback, and if he is no
  longer where the drop put him, the drill is on.

When two rules seem to apply, settle it by side first. A receiver on the far side from the scramble comes
across: deep if he was deep, and a crosser keeps crossing at his depth, toward the quarterback. On the scramble
side, short goes deep and deep comes back. Teams word this differently, but that order keeps the receivers on
different levels, which is the whole point.

**Where does the quarterback look?** The rules hand him receivers at four or five depths; he can't look at all
of them. The throws he can make while moving come first: the receiver working back toward him along his sideline,
and the crosser running with him. Both are short, firm throws toward the side he is running to. The deep
receivers are the big play, and he takes that shot when he has room to stop, set his feet and throw; a
quarterback running flat out usually can't throw 30 yards accurately. Escaping to his throwing-hand side makes all
of this easier. A right-handed quarterback rolling left has to turn his hips and square his shoulders back to the
target before he can throw at all, so for him the come-back routes on that side matter even more.

**Throw or run?** Once he is out of the pocket he has a third choice, and it is the best-valued ending in the
data, as @fig-endings will show. The rule of thumb is simple. As long as he is behind the line, his eyes stay
downfield and every receiver is still an option. When the receivers are covered and there is open grass in
front of him, ideally to the line to gain, he runs. Once he crosses the line of scrimmage the passing play is
over, because a forward pass thrown from beyond the line is illegal.[^forward-pass] Running too early gives up
the throws; running too late, after the defenders have rallied, gives up the grass.

Why does any of this work? Because the defense was built for the play the offense called, and that play is over.
Against [man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage), where each defender follows one receiver,
defenders are running with their backs to the quarterback; when a receiver stops and reverses, his defender has
to stop, turn and find him, and he is a step behind. Against
[zone coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage), where each defender guards an area,
defenders have dropped to spots that were chosen for the original routes, and they have to leave those spots to
chase receivers who are now somewhere else, opening the areas they were guarding.

The defense has rules for this too, and the scramble drill works best against a defense that breaks them. Up
front the rushers keep their [rush lanes](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) and the ends keep
[contain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contain), not rushing past the quarterback's depth, which is exactly
the mistake that opens the escape lane in @fig-pocket-moves. Some defenses assign a
[spy](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd), a defender who mirrors the quarterback and tackles him if
he runs. And in zone, once the quarterback leaves the pocket, coverage players are taught to stop guarding grass
and lock onto the nearest receiver (coaches call it "plastering"). A defense that does all of this leaves the
quarterback little; much of the off-script value in the next chart comes against defenses that don't.

``` {.python .cell-code}
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 8.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]
    dfn = four_rush() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -1.5, "W"),
                         D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -8.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 9.6, "SS"),
                         D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 15.0, "C"),
                         D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=TOGO)
    pass_set(p, depths=(-2.6, -1.7, -1.4, -1.7, -2.6))

    timed(p, "LE", [(0.8, -1.7, -5.6), (1.5, -4.6, -5.0), (2.1, -7.4, -2.2), (2.6, -8.6, 0.6), (3.3, -7.6, 5.4),

    timed(p, "NT", [(0.8, -0.6, -0.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.8, -0.7, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.8, -1.7, 4.8), (1.6, -5.8, 5.6), (2.2, -9.6, 5.6), (2.8, -11.0, 4.8), (3.6, -9.6, 8.8)], "rush")
```

The scramble drill in motion (simulated). The call is a dig by X, a shallow cross by H, a hitch route by Y and a go by Z, against man coverage with a free safety deep and a linebacker in the middle; the defense rushes four. The back, R, stays in to block, so the Will, whose man he was, has nobody to cover and mirrors the quarterback instead. Panel 1: the left end beats the left tackle (red ring). Panel 2: the quarterback escapes to his right and the receivers switch to their scramble rules. Panel 3: Z has stopped his go route and is working back down the sideline, Y has turned up the field, H keeps crossing, X comes back across deep; the quarterback throws on the run to the come-back receiver, the easy throw toward the sideline he is running at. Panel 4: Z (green ring) catches it near the sideline. His cornerback, who was running deep with his back to the quarterback, is still turning around.

**What the scramble drill solves.** A pass play is designed to finish in under three seconds. When it doesn't,
eleven offensive players are suddenly without instructions, and without rules each receiver would do something
different: some keep running their routes into the sideline, some stop, two drift into the same spot. The
scramble drill turns the broken play into a second, pre-planned play, so the quarterback's improvisation lands
on receivers who are where he expects them.

**What it gives up.** Nothing in the design, but plenty in the result: a play that goes off script is, on
average, a worse play. It is a rescue, not a strategy, and the offense would usually rather the first play had
worked. The exceptions are a handful of quarterbacks for whom the rescue is a weapon, and you can find them in
the data.
:::

### Off-script value: who gains by leaving the pocket?

FTN charts whether the quarterback was outside the pocket on each dropback, whether by design (a rollout) or by
escape; the flag does not say which. From 2022 to 2025 that happened on 18% of
NFL dropbacks. On average those plays were worth \+0\.011
[EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) (expected points added) per play, against \+0\.049
in the pocket. That average hides a split. About 48% of out-of-pocket
dropbacks ended in a quarterback run or a scramble-drill throw, and those were worth a lot; another

### A short history: from Tarkenton to Mahomes

The scramble entered the NFL's vocabulary with Fran Tarkenton, a preacher's son from Athens, Georgia, who quarterbacked
the expansion Minnesota Vikings from their first game in 1961. Behind a thin, new offensive line, he ran around
behind it, often for long stretches, until someone came open. Coaches of his era, his own first head coach Norm Van Brocklin among them, thought scrambling undisciplined (the feud with Van Brocklin ended with Tarkenton demanding a trade in 1967);
Tarkenton's answer, preserved on his Hall of Fame page, was that "I scramble because I'm good at it, because I can
twist and dodge those big pass rushers better than most guys, and we get a lot of touchdowns that way." He retired
in 1978 holding the career records for completions, passing yards and touchdown passes.[^tarkenton]

For decades after that the pocket passer was the ideal: the quarterbacks who won the most, from Joe Montana to
Peyton Manning and Tom Brady, did their damage on schedule, and the offenses built around them, timed to the drop,
treated a scramble as a play that had failed. But the off-script line never died. John Elway passed for 3,000 yards
and ran for 200 in seven straight seasons and built a career on late comebacks; Steve Young retired with 43 rushing
touchdowns, then the second-most by any quarterback.[^offscript-hof] Teams with quarterbacks like them practiced what
to do when the play broke.

What changed in the last decade is scale. College football filled with spread offenses and athletic quarterbacks who
had been improvising since high school, and NFL offenses stopped treating the scramble drill as an emergency
procedure and started repping it weekly and designing around it. The quarterbacks who came out of that world
(Mahomes, Allen, Lamar Jackson, Jalen Hurts) made off-script play part of the plan rather than an emergency.

## Getting rid of it: the throwaway

The last of the quarterback's options when nothing is open is the least glamorous and among the most valuable. A
[**throwaway**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-throwaway) is a pass he deliberately throws where nobody can
catch it, usually out of bounds or well over a covered receiver's head, to avoid a sack or an interception. He
gives up the down but keeps the yards. NFL quarterbacks threw the ball away on
3\.5% of dropbacks from 2022 to 2025.

Why is that a skill and not a surrender? Look at what the alternatives cost. In the same seasons, the average
throwaway was worth \-0\.78 EPA (an incompletion, a lost down), the average sack
\-1\.77 (a lost down *and* six or seven yards), and the average interception
\-4\.42. A quarterback who turns two sacks a game into throwaways gains about
2 points a game for his team, without completing a pass.

There is a catch, and it is a rule. [**Intentional grounding**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-grounding) is a foul for throwing the ball away to avoid a sack
when the pass isn't in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver; it costs a loss of down and ten yards
(or loss of down at the spot of the pass, if that is worse), and a safety if the quarterback throws it from his own end zone. The
rule changes once the quarterback leaves the
[**tackle box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-box), the area between where the two offensive tackles
lined up: outside it, any pass that lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage (including out of bounds past it) is
legal, receiver or no receiver.[^grounding] [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)
covers the full rule; here is what it means for the quarterback.

The rule rewards exactly the skills this chapter has been describing. A quarterback who climbs and slides inside the
pocket can always find a covered receiver to throw near; a quarterback who escapes the pocket earns the right to
throw it into the stands. The quarterback who gets in trouble is the one who stays in the box with nobody near
him, panics, and flings it at the turf, or who, outside the box, tries to throw it away on the run and doesn't get
it back to the line.

The most famous grounding call of recent decades shows how expensive the panic is. On the New England Patriots' first
offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, against the New York Giants in February 2012, Tom Brady dropped back from his
own 6-yard line with Justin Tuck bearing down on him, and threw deep down the middle to nobody. The flag came out;
Brady had thrown it from his own end zone, so the grounding penalty was a safety, and the Giants, who had punted
on their own opening drive, led 2-0. They won by four.[^xlvi]

## The checkdown: risk management, not cowardice {#checkdown}

The last read in most progressions is the [**checkdown**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown): a short,
safe throw, usually to a running back or tight end a few yards past the line, underneath all the coverage. It is
the quarterback giving up on the big play to take a small, nearly certain one. Fans boo it. Coaches mostly
don't, and the data says why.

Read @fig-endings from the middle out. A checkdown is worth, on average, \+0\.03
EPA: essentially nothing. It is caught 82% of the time, thrown about
0\.6 yards past the line, and gains most of what it gains after the catch
(6\.3 yards on average). That looks like a wasted play only if you compare it to the first
read. The real comparison is to what happens to a quarterback who *doesn't* check the ball down when the first
reads are covered: he holds it, and the next three bars are waiting. The checkdown is the cheapest way to end a
play that has failed.

That is what *risk management* means at quarterback. Each read in the progression has an expected value and a
risk of disaster, and the checkdown is the read with the least of both. A quarterback who takes it at the right
moment gives up a little upside to cut off the tail of sacks and interceptions, and over a season that tail decides
games.

The right moment depends on the situation, and the third-down numbers show how much (2022–2025, share of plays
that gained the first down, and EPA):

| Third down, and the ball goes… | Converted | EPA per play |
|---|---|---|
| 7+ yards to go: to the first read | 43% | – |
| 7+ yards to go: checked down | 24% | \-0\.20 |
| 7+ yards to go: sacked | 0% | \-1\.79 |
| 3 or fewer to go: checked down | 58% | – |

On third-and-long, a checkdown usually means a punt. Even so it beats the sack: when the ball is going to be punted
anyway, the yards the back gains after the catch still flip a little field position, while a sack can push a field
goal out of range. On third-and-short the same throw is a good bet. Good quarterbacks know the down and distance on
every snap and adjust: checkdowns early, when four yards on first down keeps the offense
[on schedule](../10-situational-football/10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd), patience on third-and-long,
when only a throw past the sticks will do.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Checking it down is what scared quarterbacks do." Every great quarterback checks the ball down, often, and good
offenses design their checkdowns to gain yards: a back who catches it in space with one linebacker to beat. The difference between a good checkdown and a bad one is
*when*: a checkdown after the deeper reads were honestly covered is a good decision; a checkdown on the first beat
of a play, before the deep reads had time to open, is a quarterback who has stopped trusting his protection.
Watch where his eyes were before he threw it.
:::

## Measuring a quarterback: time to throw, aDOT, CPOE and EPA

You can now describe a quarterback's process. The data can describe his *style* and his *results*, and four
numbers do most of the work.

- **[Time to throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-time-to-throw)** (seconds from the snap to the release)
  says how long he holds the ball: quick and decisive, or patient and hunting.
- **[aDOT](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-adot)** (average depth of target) says how far downfield he aims:
  underneath and safe, or deep and aggressive.
- **CPOE** says how accurate he is, after allowing for how hard his throws were.
- **EPA per dropback** says what it all adds up to: the points his dropbacks added, sacks, scrambles and turnovers
  included.

The first two describe style, and neither is good or bad on its own; the last two describe results. All four are
public: the Next Gen Stats passing leaderboard (<https://nextgenstats.nfl.com/stats/passing>) has time to throw,
air yards and its own CPOE for every starter, and rbsdm.com (<https://rbsdm.com/stats/>), built on the same
nflverse data as this chapter, has EPA per dropback and CPOE, so you can profile this Sunday's quarterback before
kickoff. The one that needs explaining is CPOE.

### CPOE: completion percentage, corrected for difficulty

Completion percentage is the oldest quarterback number and one of the most misleading, because it rewards easy
throws. A quarterback who checks the ball down all day completes 75% of his passes; one who throws deep outs and
posts completes 60% and may be the better passer. **[CPOE](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cpoe)**, or
**[completion percentage over expected](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-completion-percentage-over-expected)**,
fixes this by comparing each throw with a model's estimate of how often a throw like it is completed. The nflverse
model behind the numbers here knows each throw's depth, which part of the field it went to, the down and distance,
and whether the quarterback was hit as he threw;[^cp-model] the Next Gen Stats version also knows, from tracking
data, how far the receiver was from the nearest defender.[^ngs-xcomp] A deep out to the sideline might have an
expected completion rate of 45%; a checkdown to the flat, 85%. Complete the deep out and you gain 55 percentage
points over expected; drop the checkdown and you lose 85. Average those differences over a season and you have CPOE.

::: {#cell-fig-cpoe .cell execution_count=13}

CPOE is the best single public measure of accuracy, and it is steadier from season to season than completion
percentage, but read it with three cautions. It credits the quarterback for everything that is not in the model: a
receiver who makes a great catch, or a scheme that gets receivers wide open, raises it. It says nothing about
*where* the ball went, only whether it was caught: a quarterback who throws safely and accurately to covered
checkdowns can post a fine CPOE and a poor offense. And check what each version does with throwaways. They count
as incompletions in plain completion percentage, which punishes a smart habit, but the nflverse model leaves most
of them out, because only 18% of charted throwaways get a completion
probability.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Completion percentage measures accuracy." It measures accuracy *and* the difficulty of the throws a quarterback
chooses, mixed together, and difficulty dominates. A conservative passer and an aggressive one can be equally
accurate and be ten points apart in completion percentage. If you want accuracy, look at CPOE; if you want to know
how aggressive he is, look at aDOT; if you want to know whether it worked, look at EPA.
:::

### Whose sack is it?

Sacks are charged to the quarterback's line in the box score, but a good share of them belong to him. FTN's
charters, who watch every sack on video, marked 40% of the sacks from 2022 to 2025
as the quarterback's fault: held the ball too long, drifted into the rush, missed the hot throw. A cleaner number
separates the line's share from his: *pressure-to-sack rate*, the share of the dropbacks on which he was
[pressured](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure) that ended in a sack. The line decides how often he is
pressured; what happens next is mostly him. From 2023 to 2025 pressured quarterbacks were sacked
22% of the time, but among those with 200 or more pressured dropbacks the rate ran
from 13% (Nix) to
30% (Levis).[^p2s] That spread is
pocket presence, measured. [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) takes up why pressure is the
steadier number and the sack the noisier one.
